newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels hold swathe of territory in the east.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels hold swathe of territory in the east.

text.p: A swathe of territory in eastern Zaire from Lake Tanganyika to Lake Kivu was in rebel hands on Thursday and the rebels vowed to fight on until they ousted President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Thousands of victorious and heavily armed Banyamulenge fighters were visible on the road as I travelled south with the rebels from the town of Kamanyola, near Bukavu, to the town of Uvira, about 100 km (60 miles) south.
Zairean refugees, belongings piled on their heads, returned on foot to their homes in the town, which seemed largely intact because rebels said Zairean forces simply fled.
I and another foreign journalist who arrived in Uvira on Thursday were the first to visit the lakeside city since it was seized by rebel forces a week ago.

As we drove into town in a convoy escorted by Banyamulenge fighters, people cheered at roadsides. Thousands of chanting Uvira residents later attended a rally by the rebels who urged them to join their struggle against Zairean strongman Mobutu.

"The alliance appeals to the rest of the Zairean population to rise up against the repressive system that has plunged the people of this country into misery," Laurent Kabila, chief coordinator of the newly formed Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, told the cheering crowd.
"This is your movement. It is a movement against tyranny and corruption. It is a movement for freedom and human life."
Kabila, speaking in Swahili, said the struggle against Mobutu would be long, but he told the crowd victory was certain.
"We must remove Mobutu and throw him into the dustbin of history," said Kabila, a stout 56-year-old veteran of a rebellion crushed by Mobutu's forces in the 1960s.

He said Zaire had totally collapsed under Mobutu and it would take hard work, commitment and sacrifice to restore the nation to order. He accused Mobutu of gross human rights abuses and promised that the alliance would restore law and order.
Kabila earlier reeled off at a news conference the rebel military victories and objectives. He said rebel forces entered Bukavu at 1 a.m. on Thursday and seized a large part of town.

"Our forces are advancing on all government positions...A large part of Bukavu is now under our control and our forces are mopping up pockets of resistance from ex-FAR and Interahamwe militia," he said at his headquarters in an abandoned home.

The FAR is the former Rwandan Hutu government army which played a leading role in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda and fled into exile in Zaire before Tutsi rebels seized power. Interahamwe Hutu militiamen also helped lead the mass slaughter.

"Goma is in the process of falling as I talk to you. Government forces are running away. There is a big battle going on in Goma and within two days we will have full control of the city," Kabila said.
"Goma airport is under the control of our military forces," said the rebel leader.
He said after Goma was captured the advance would continue until rebel forces reached the capital Kinshasa, 1,600 km (1,000 miles) west of Goma. There is no road from Kinshasa to Goma.
Kabila, surrounded by gun-toting guards, said after heavy fighting for a commando base in Kamanyola the only real resistance met by the rebels in Uvira was from Burundian Hutu rebels.
The Banyamulenge, who moved to what is now Zaire from what is now Rwanda up to 200 years ago, say they launched their rebellion to stop a campaign of genocide against them by the Zairean military.
Their lightning offensive started in South Kivu province with Kamanyola among the first towns to fall last week, followed by Uvira. They then thrust northwards and moved on Bukavu.
Asked about Zairean accusations the rebels were supported by Rwanda, Kabila said:
"We are not supported by Rwanda or anyone externally. Zairean soldiers have lost territory and continue to lose it because they are totally demoralised, depressed and cannot therefore fight."
